newsitem.title: FINLAND: HARD TO READ MUCH IN CHEAPENING NEWSPRINT - ANALYSTS.
newsitem.headline: HARD TO READ MUCH IN CHEAPENING NEWSPRINT - ANALYSTS.

text.p: It is nearly 18 months since Rupert Murdoch made a much-publicised visit to Finland "to beg for paper", but he and other media moguls face a much easier time getting supplies at least next year, analysts say.
Prices for newsprint, already under pressure after ramping up by 50 percent last year and trimming publishers' margins all round, are headed clearly downwards in Europe, analysts say.

But while some say at least 20 percent could be chopped off current prices, others warn the supply-demand balance is very delicate and anyway lower paper prices will not automatically translate into an equivalent profit boost for newsprint users.
On the price side, few forest industry analysts see any alternative but for newsprint prices to retreat sharply.

"The outlook for newsprint looks poor, to put it mildly," said Lars Kjellberg, forest industry analyst at Enskilda in Sweden. Extra capacity in Asia is shrinking world leader Canada's export markets, so they are dumping product in Europe.

"Newsprint prices on the U.S. east cost are about $530 per tonne while in Germany they are around $790 per tonne, so it is quite obvious that a lot of Canadian paper is coming to Europe," said Kjellberg.
The cost of shipping newsprint paper over the Atlantic is about $40 per tonne, he said.
He expects Canadian shipments to Europe to increase by some 200,000 to 230,000 tonnes next year, and on top of this sees an increase of some 100,000 to 250,000 tonnes from Russia.
"In all, that equals (the output of) one and a half paper machines," he said, forecasting a drop in European prices, now around 1,220-1,225 German marks (about $792 to $795).
"I think prices will in 1997-98 stabilise at around 950 to 1,000 marks," he said.
Anticipation of this has been one factor behind clear underperformance in the stock of Europe's biggest forestry group UPM-Kymmene Oy's in Helsinki since early last month.

Although it managed a rise on Thursday, at 93.60 markka it is back near where it started the year, after peaking in August at 105.00 -- against a 30 percent increase for the Helsinki general index to date.
Niels Leth, forestry analyst at Den Danske Bank in Copenhagen, added another bearish factor: "I believe that sooner or later we will se a fall in consumption of newsprint."
He cited signs of falling demand in North America: on the one hand this could be due to recent high costs, but he also believes electronic media will eventually curb newspaper use.

For Leth, a key question on when newsprint prices would recover is if Canada's producers decide, once prices are not enough to cover their relatively high costs, to close down some of their older and less efficient machines.
"We believe a 15-20 percent (price) fall from current levels would be enough for them to start asking themselves (whether to close down the machines)," he said.
If they did, 1998 could be the turnaround year.

But for newspaper publishers like News Corp Ltd , Pearson or Springer , analysts say cheaper paper may be an invitation to publish advertising supplements for a growing army of consumers as economic growth gains pace.
Newsprint makes up about 30 percent of the cost of national newspapers in Britain, said Anthony de Larrinaga, analyst at Panmure Gordon in London.
"It's a very fine balance here and it can lead to some wild swings," he said. "It's worse than trying to guess oil prices."

"I wouldn't factor in 20 percent (lower newsprint prices) for my budgets on the companies -- you would be perhaps a hostage to fortune ... it would be taking a big risk, putting such an aggressive forecast in," he said.
